newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU edges closer to ruling against Boeing-McDonnell merger.
newsitem.headline: EU edges closer to ruling against Boeing-McDonnell merger.

text.p: Antitrust experts from across Europe unanimously advised the European Union on Wednesday to rule against the $14 billion Boeing Co.-McDonnell Douglas Corp. merger, setting the stage for a trans-Atlantic dispute.
Their call was echoed by political leaders in Germany and France, with French President Jacques Chirac saying the merger could be "dangerous" for European industry.
But members of Congress denounced the EU stance as outrageous.

"I am outraged," said Sen. Slade Gorton, a Republican from Boeing's home state of Washington. "The Europeans are asserting antitrust authority in an extraterritorial manner where there is no relevance, other than the fact that we sell airplanes in their market."

At the White House, spokesman Mike McCurry measured his words carefully: "We think the principles of competitiveness are those that ought to attend to the European Union's consideration" of the merger. He added that the decision should "be done consistently with antitrust law as it's applied within the (European) Union."

EU officials said they did not expect a compromise ahead of a meeting next Wednesday when the EU's executive commission is to make its final decision on the merger, which would solidify Boeing's position as the world's largest commercial aircraft maker.

"The advisory committee agreed with the commission that the commitments offered by the parties to date are not sufficient to remedy the competition problems," an EU source said following a daylong meeting of the antitrust experts.

German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt also threw his support behind the commission. Germany's Daimler-Benz Aerospace and France's Aerospatiale are the main partners in Airbus Industrie, the European plane maker that is Boeing's main rival.
Airbus has said the merger is part of a strategy, with the complicity of Washington, to eliminate it altogether.
Despite the strong EU stance, Boeing said it would stick to its guns by refusing to make further concessions.

"We have negotiated in good faith. We have taken very seriously each of the commission's concerns and have made a sincere effort to put forward substantial remedies in each of the areas," Boeing's vice president for European affairs, Jim Frank, said in an interview.

Industry officials and experts in EU competition law have been sceptical the commission would move to ban the merger outright. While it may rule against the deal, some lawyers have said Boeing would probably refile an amended merger plan.
The deal has been cleared without conditions in the United States, but it needs regulatory approval in the EU because of the amount of business Boeing does in the 15-country bloc.
Were Boeing to ignore a ruling against it, the commission could fine it up to 10 percent of sales and fine European companies doing business with the Seattle-based aicraft maker.
Commission sources said the EU could also seize any new planes being delivered in Europe.
The current stalemate raised the specter of a bitter trans-Atlantic dispute.
Vice President Al Gore warned recently that the Clinton administration would take any appropriate action to prevent the commission from torpedoing the merger.
Rexrodt said Boeing had not fully addressed concerns about its exclusive supply contracts with major U.S. airlines and the danger that military funds and technology would spill into civilian areas.

European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert has criticised the merger since it was announced in December, saying Boeing's long-term contracts with American Airlines, Continental Airlines and Delta Air Lines were unacceptable.
Boeing offered not to sign new exclusive supply deals for 10 years and to scale back existing contracts, but Rexrodt said the company's offers were insufficient.
